reading.body:
The AFL-CIO's AI lobbying footprint is 7 filings, 10 named lobbyists, and 28 distinct bills, all from 2025 or later.

The pattern is breadth over depth. One client, the AFL-CIO, appears across all 7 filings, and the lobbyist counts fall off steeply: one lobbyist on 7 filings, one on 4, one on 3, four on 2, and two on 1. The bill list is longer than the lobbyist list, which means the federation is spreading a small team across a wide set of legislation rather than concentrating on a few measures.

For AI specifically, this is labor's presence in the federal AI policy fight. The bills named span both chambers, with 16 House bills and 12 Senate bills, and the filings are recent enough that they describe active 2025 legislation rather than settled law. Lobbying on AI is not only a technology-industry activity.

What the data does not say is what the AFL-CIO argued. A filing reports that a client lobbied on an issue, not the position taken, so nothing here indicates whether the federation supported, opposed, or sought to amend any bill. The data also does not connect these filings to data centers, power procurement, or grid policy, so no claim about compute or electricity can be drawn from it.

summary: AFL-CIO filed 7 Lobbying Disclosure Act reports on AI held by this site. Its clients, the lobbyists named on those filings and the AI bills they name are below. LDA registrant id 363.
